title: A One-Two Punch Has Atlantic Hurricane Season on the Ropes
gist: A record-intensifying El Niño plus Saharan dry-dust intrusions and a weak West African monsoon are suppressing the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, on track to be the quietest since at least 2013 with an ACE of just 3.1 (23% of the mid-August average). The same conditions are driving a hyperactive western Pacific typhoon season, the busiest by early August in nearly 50 years.

insights.claim: The Atlantic basin has seen only three weak named storms since June, with forecasters now expecting fewer than 10 named storms and the least active season since at least 2013.
insights.speaker: Dennis Mersereau
insights.so_what: A quiet season lowers near-term catastrophe-insurance loss expectations and Gulf energy-disruption risk.

insights.claim: The 2026 season has produced an Accumulated Cyclone Energy of 3.1 versus an average full-season ACE of 122.5, just 23 percent of average for mid-August.
insights.speaker: Dennis Mersereau
insights.so_what: A quantified activity collapse is a hard input for reinsurance and commodity-risk models.

insights.claim: This year's El Niño has intensified with unprecedented speed, running at least 1.5°C above average in a key equatorial Pacific region with anomalies up to 4°C, driving stronger wind shear east over the Atlantic that disrupts budding tropical systems.
insights.speaker: Dennis Mersereau
insights.so_what: The physical mechanism linking Pacific warming to Atlantic quiet is the key driver forecasters and insurers track.

insights.claim: Saharan dry, dusty air intrusions act like a lid suppressing thunderstorm development, and a lackluster West African monsoon with below-average rainfall in Sierra Leone and Guinea is producing weaker seed disturbances.
insights.speaker: Dennis Mersereau
insights.so_what: Multiple compounding suppressors reinforce confidence in a benign Atlantic season.

insights.claim: The western Pacific typhoon season was busier by early August than any season in almost 50 years, with four storms reaching Category 5 equivalent including Sinlaku in April and Bavi, Dolphin, and Genevieve in July.
insights.speaker: Dennis Mersereau
insights.so_what: The same El Niño quieting the Atlantic elevates Pacific-basin disaster and supply-chain risk in Asia.

insights.claim: Fewer storms doesn't mean zero: this year's Tropical Storm Arthur may have broken Louisiana's 24-hour rainfall record with over 29 inches near Cottonport, and past El Niño years produced intense hurricanes like Camille, Ivan, Charley, Michael, Idalia, and Lee.
insights.speaker: Dennis Mersereau
insights.so_what: A low-frequency season can still deliver a single catastrophic landfall, so coastal loss tail-risk remains.
